Addressed by #41204. Each Location-scoped MCP service now subscribes to `config.updated`, compares the previous and next effective server maps, and reconciles only entries that were added, removed, disabled, or materially changed. Replacement closes the old configured runtime without disturbing unrelated or API-registered servers; unchanged config does not restart connections, and startup reconciliation is installed after the live subscription so updates cannot be missed. Focused MCP tests cover the reconciliation behavior. Closing as resolved on the v2 branch.

> Additional data point from a local TypeScript plugin setup on 1.18.15 (Windows):
>
> Same root cause, two different error strings depending on the shape of the named exports:
>
> - `export function` / `export const` named exports + `export default` plugin function
>   → log: `Plugin export is not a function` (exact match with this issue)
> - plugin with ONLY builtin imports (`fs`, `path`) + named exports + `export default`
>   → log: `The "paths[0]" property must be of type string, got object`
>
> The second message is very misleading — it looks like a module-resolution failure but is actually the same `getLegacyPlugins` path rejecting a non-function named export.
>
> Workaround confirmed: removing every named export (keeping only `export default`) makes the plugin load correctly.
>
> Suggested fix (1) from the issue — skip non-plugin-shaped exports instead of throwing — would cover both messages.

Thanks for updating your PR! It now meets our contributing guidelines. :+1:

## Technical details

### Root cause

The SSE consumer in `packages/app/src/context/server-sdk.tsx` reads the response body with no timeout. A socket that dies without a FIN/RST (nginx `proxy_read_timeout`, NAT eviction, Cloudflare 100s window, host suspend) parks `reader.read()` forever — no error is thrown, so the reconnect loop is never re-entered. Heartbeats can't help at the event level because the v2 server sends them as SSE comment frames, which the SSE parser discards without yielding an event. Evidence in #40910: nginx log shows `upstream prematurely closed connection ... GET /global/event`, and access logs show the stream alternating between healthy long-lived responses and ones that end almost immediately.

### Why byte-level tracking is required

A watchdog reset on parsed *events* (the approach in #41002) kills healthy idle streams: when a session is quiet, the only traffic on the wire is heartbeat comment frames, which never produce events. With a 45s event-based watchdog, every idle session would be disconnected and reconnected every 45 seconds. Tracking bytes through a fetch wrapper keeps quiet-but-healthy streams alive while still detecting dead ones.

### Why the repair is transport-driven

`reconcileActiveSessionStatuses` must not wait for a `server.connected` frame — the whole failure mode is a stream that stops delivering, so a repair that waits to be told about the reconnect is exactly the one that never runs. The `onReconnect` hook fires on the attempt itself, before any byte arrives, and the repair goes over plain HTTP (`session.active()` / `session.status()`), so it works even if the replacement stream also dies. It also deliberately bypasses `activeSessionsQuery`: a first fetch that never settles would otherwise leave the repair permanently skipped (refetch dedupes onto the wedged request).

### Changes

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `server-sdk.tsx` (+99) | `createActivityTrackingFetch` byte-tracking wrapper; per-attempt stall watchdog (45s / 5s check) capturing the attempt's `AbortController`; `onReconnect` hook on the event API |
| `server-sync.tsx` (+82) | `reconcileActiveSessionStatuses` (clear stale `busy`, force-resync sessions holding messages); `repairAfterReconnect` wired to `onReconnect`; bootstrap path reconciles too |
| `server-sdk.test.ts` (+46) | heartbeat byte-tracking, non-stream passthrough |
| `server-sync.test.ts` (+61) | finished-run cleanup, message-only resync, racing bootstrap recovery |

### Relationship to earlier PRs

- #41002 (watchdog-only): reconnects the transport but never repairs drifted state — runs that finished during the outage keep spinning until a manual refresh, so it doesn't fully resolve #40910. Also resets on events, which churns idle connections every 45s.
- #39349 (byte-tracking + repair): correct direction; this PR keeps that mechanism and additionally updates `activity` on every parsed event as a fallback, and drives the repair solely from the transport hook (avoiding double repair from both the hook and the `server.connected` handler).

Same root cause also reported in #39030, #39352, #38458, #32175 — this fix covers them as well.

## Community tool available: opencode-db-prune

For anyone hitting this issue right now (and it seems like many are), I built a standalone tool that safely reclaims this space without waiting for upstream changes:

**https://github.com/ANGELBERRIOS23/opencode-db-prune**

Single Python file, stdlib only, no dependencies. What it does:

- **Report mode by default** — shows exactly what would be pruned, changes nothing
- **Deletes only redundant event snapshots** (`message.updated.1`, `message.part.updated.1`, `session.updated.1`) — never touches sessions, messages, or file parts
- **Safety checks**: refuses to run if DB is open, verifies content is readable outside `event`, runs `PRAGMA integrity_check` before and after, backs up first
- **Keeps N newest sessions untouched** (configurable via `--keep`)
- **Cross-platform**: macOS tested, Linux/Windows implemented

Results on a real installation:
- 39.37 GB → 3.15 GB (36 GB reclaimed)
- All 2,106 sessions, 59,294 messages, 293,777 file parts intact
- `integrity_check`: ok

```bash
python3 opencode-db-prune.py              # report only
python3 opencode-db-prune.py --apply      # prune with backup
python3 opencode-db-prune.py --apply --keep 20
```

This is meant as a bridge until the proper fix lands upstream. Happy to collaborate on integrating the approach into the core CLI (similar to what PR #36710 proposes, but available today as a standalone tool).

Would love feedback from anyone who tries it on Linux or Windows.

Requesting reopen — still relevant, and the branch is now rebased and conflict-free.

**Rebased onto current `dev`** (`fe82a1b`). The branch was 206 commits behind; the three `Merge branch 'dev'` commits are now flattened into a single feature commit (`0a8a54b`). The rebase applied with no conflicts, and `tsgo --noEmit` is clean for `packages/opencode` (the only package this PR touches).

**The gap this closes is still open today.** Checked against both sources just now:

- `models.dev` lists **95** Abacus models
- the Abacus `/v1/models` endpoint returns **153** models, **74** of them `model_type: text_generation`
- **12** of those 74 are absent from `models.dev` — including `claude-opus-5`, `moonshotai/Kimi-K3`, `moonshotai/Kimi-K2.7-Code`, `gemini-3.6-flash`, `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731` and `thinkingmachines/Inkling`

Without discovery those models are simply unreachable from opencode unless the user hand-maintains a local models database and points `OPENCODE_MODELS_PATH` at it, which is the workaround I'm running today. The set drifts every few weeks as Abacus adds models, so it's a standing maintenance cost rather than a one-time gap in `models.dev`.

**The second half of the PR is provider-agnostic.** It replaces the hardcoded `gitlab` branch in the discovery step with a generic loop over `discoveryLoaders`, so any provider returning `discoverModels` gets picked up without extra wiring. That block is still hardcoded on `dev` today (`packages/opencode/src/provider/provider.ts:1598`).

Happy to split this into two PRs — the generic `discoveryLoaders` loop on its own, then the Abacus loader on top — if that's easier to review.

Another reproducible data point on OpenCode `1.18.15` with `@ai-sdk/openai-compatible`: a transient error delivered **inside an already-established SSE stream** terminates the turn without entering session retry.

The provider emits an SSE error shaped like:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "message": "Upstream HTTP/2 stream failed",
    "type": "upstream_error",
    "code": "upstream_http2_stream_error"
  }
}
```

Observed OpenCode logs contain exactly one `message=stream`, followed by `message="stream error"`, `process error`, and pruning. There is no retry status and no second `message=stream`. The upstream request is therefore attempted once, with zero retries.

The apparent normalization path is:

1. The OpenAI-compatible adapter forwards `chunk.value.error` as a plain object.
2. `MessageV2.fromError()` calls `ProviderError.parseStreamError()`.
3. `parseStreamError()` requires `body.type === "error"`, but the unwrapped object has `type === "upstream_error"`, so parsing returns `undefined`.
4. The object becomes `UnknownError`.
5. Its serialized message does not match the current retry patterns (`upstream connect`, stream timeout, etc.), so `SessionRetry.retryable()` returns `undefined`.

This is adjacent to, but not the same layer as, the transport/socket errors described in this issue. It appears to be the same class as #21893, which is currently closed. Could a maintainer confirm whether #21893 should be reopened, or whether a narrowly scoped issue/PR for structured SSE errors would be preferred?

A safe fix should avoid blindly replaying a stream after text or tool calls have already been emitted. Retrying only before any assistant output/tool call, with a small attempt cap, would avoid duplicate side effects.

This is related to #17372 and #30615, but the specific issue here is the PowerShell 7 MSIX App Execution Alias.

PowerShell 7 is installed through the standard Microsoft Store/MSIX package, and the normal WindowsApps PATH entry resolves `pwsh` correctly in Windows Terminal. OpenCode does not recognize that alias during shell discovery.

Adding the version-specific package directory under `C:\Program Files\WindowsApps` makes OpenCode detect PowerShell 7, which strongly suggests that the issue is in executable discovery and validation rather than in the PATH configuration itself.

I have more data from the same VPS host (contabo) that isolates where the TUI startup time goes.

## TUI terminal query (Ghostty fix)

The blocking palette query discussed earlier can be worked around with an undocumented env var:

```
OTUI_PALETTE_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS=1
```

On my VPS this cuts ~4.5s from TUI startup (from ~11.9s to ~7.5s TTFD). The query logic is in `packages/core/src/lib/terminal-palette.ts`. This is a TUI-only issue -- CLI subcommands like `--version` and `debug config` are not affected.

Another undocumented flag, `OPENCODE_FAST_BOOT` (`packages/tui/src/app.tsx`: `skipInitialLoading`), skips the initial loading screen and reduces TTFD to ~2.7s, but the UI is not fully ready for another 3-4s.

## Remaining TUI startup cost

After fixing the terminal query with `OTUI_PALETTE_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS=1`, the TUI still takes ~7.5s TTFD on my VPS. About 1.5s is the static import tree (#24868) paid before the TUI even starts, and ~0.8s is the config/skill loader walking ~41 skill directories sequentially. The rest is the TUI render cycle (providers, contexts, route resolution).

## Suggestions (v2 codebase)

Looking at the `2.0` branch, the TUI still exists at `packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/tui/` alongside the new web UI and desktop apps:

### 1. Terminal query: may already be fixed in v2

`terminal-palette.ts` is absent from the v2 tree. If the palette query was removed or restructured, this entire 4.5s delay disappears for v2 TUI users. 

### 2. Reduce the pre-TUI floor

The v2 entrypoint (`packages/opencode/src/index.ts`) still has 38 eager imports, same as v1. Lazy-loading subcommand handlers would cut the fixed ~1.5s cost before the TUI even begins rendering. This was suggested in #24868 but closed as not planned for v1 -- v2 is a clean opportunity to adopt it.

### 3. Parallel skill discovery

The config loader walks skill directories sequentially (~0.8s on a slow VPS core). Skills from different directories do not need ordering relative to each other. A two-phase approach (discover paths in parallel, then merge in order) would let the loader use more than 1.6 cores.

### 4. Document the workarounds

`OTUI_PALETTE_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` and `OPENCODE_FAST_BOOT` are undocumented. Documenting them (or promoting them to config options) would reduce "slow startup" reports from v1 TUI users.

### Additional impact scenario: dirty working tree during Git push

I encountered a concrete consequence of this issue on Linux with OpenCode 1.18.15:

1. Two OpenCode TUI instances were running in the same project directory. I did not realize the other instance was still writing files.
2. Instance A modified files through a background subagent.
3. Instance B prepared a Git push, detected the dirty working tree, and correctly refused to push.
4. OpenCode never warned that another instance was active in the same workspace.

The fail-closed Git behavior prevented an inconsistent push, but the root cause was invisible until the logs were correlated. A visible warning when opening a second instance, as proposed here, would have prevented the confusion.

No subagent cancellation occurred; both background tasks completed normally. This is specifically an instance-awareness and workspace-coordination problem.
